chunks: "Inrush current is the large surge a load draws at the moment it's turned on, before it settles to its normal running current.
For a motor it happens because, at standstill, there's no back-EMF.
The only thing limiting current is the winding resistance, so you get roughly V over R, which can be many times the running current.
In my example, a 12 volt, 1 ohm motor running at 5 amps under load would start at up to about 12 amps, and with no load the ratio is 20 or more.
It lasts until the rotor speeds up and the back-EMF builds, tens of milliseconds for a small motor.
The inductance does smooth the first few milliseconds, but doesn't remove the peak.
For solenoids on DC the max is just the steady current, but AC solenoids have a large inrush when the plunger is open because the impedance is low.
Other loads have inrush for other reasons: capacitors charging, cold lamp filaments, transformer cores. It matters because the supply, wiring and driver see that peak.
A battery with internal resistance sags, which can reset a microcontroller. A fuse or current limit can trip.
To handle it you use soft start, ramping the PWM duty, a current limit in the driver, series resistance or an NTC thermistor, and bulk capacitors near the logic."
